Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: My boss offered me a role with more responsibility with no increase in pay, implying it's "good for your career" and that my chances of a raise are higher, what would you think/do?
Answer: Take it. Make sure it comes with a better title. If you don't eventually get more pay commensurate with your new position, your boss has at least given you the ticket to getting more pay at your next employer. More responsibility is generally very good for your career regardless of pay. There is a question if you want to do that job that you will have to answer for yourself, but this is a good career move on all other accounts. Few companies will ever hire you into a higher position then the one you are leaving unless they are a startup and desperate. Other companies will almost certainly pay you more though if they want you. What you have been given is priceless in terms of career development. Worry about the money after you have delivered on your new title and find yourself undervalued and with new opportunity to get more pay elsewhere.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What do liberal progressives think about the living conditions in San Francisco?
Answer: Ugh. It turns out the romanticized moral of the story of David vs Goliath is, in general, profoundly bad. San Francisco is your evidence. It turns out, big slow moving entities that sometimes harm the little guy often do so for the greater good. The proverbial David may have been smaller and protecting a minority, but he crushed Goliath then used his righteous indignation as justification to force his Christian identity on the Pagan majority. A similar thing happens in San Francisco. I was driving through the city this weekend, coming from the south bay. I didn’t want to do anything in the city, just get through it as quickly as possible. That’s just not possible. San Francisco hates cars. I do too, but that doesn’t change the reality we currently live in. California has been seeing massive growth for the better part of a century and seeing the problems of rapid growth during the age of the automobile is most acute here. San Francisco’s hate of cars is a long held belief thats been in place since the 60s when highway 101 and 280 was being built and had plans to cut through the west side of San Francisco. Growth and cars bring lots of problems with it. Cars may not be the best solution particularly in urban areas, but they are a net benefit over nothing. Of course more cars means lots of changes, that will have some very adverse effects on individuals. Houses would be lost, public places would be disturbed. It sucks, especially so for the handful of individuals who live in the path of that highway. I am a vocal advocate for building more public transportation and prioritizing walkability and bike lanes over highways and street parking, but I also have the common sense to realize thats a slow change that requires massive agreement on zoning and infrastructure to happen over time. Not building a single section of highway is simply not a viable option when the rest of the state has already made it the defacto transportation mechanism. The entire Bay Area is built for cars and the highways are how everyone gets around as there really are no other good options for a majority of uses case. In any case, protests in the 60s were successful. Despite the plans for the highway that were open for public comment and went through years of permitting and a drawn out planning process to find the least disruptive compromise, days before concrete was to start pouring another city council vote triggered by massive protests passed on a 6 to 5 vote cemented the lack of a highway to this day. For the perceived benefit of a handful of NIMBYs, everyone who lives in the area has to deal with significantly increased commute times. Unfortunately those protests were not “lets find a better transportation solution that works for everyone”, they simply found fault with an imperfect proposed solution and left it at that. No effort was expended to address how to better correct the worsening growth problems the solution was targeting. To this day, highway 101 ends in San Francisco, then continues after you get past it. The trouble is, even though, the highway doesn’t exist, the traffic still does. Traffic from a 12-lane highway is dumped onto city streets with lights and lots of cross traffic whether you want to end up there or not. Everyone, including the NIMBYs still lose. Ultimately the city has to deal with a massive amount of cars for longer. The noise, the pollution, the danger, the time wasted is all worse then it would of been by building a highway correctly. Cars remain in the city for more time. Public transportation also remains largely unsuccessful as the rest of the Bay Area doesn’t have the density along the transportation corridor to support it. 50 years on, demand for highways has only increased. It turns out that Goliath is big and less sympathetic to individual concerns because it has to be, not because it is inherently evil. Highways are the natural extension of how you support people who want to live in low density suburbs. That is but one anecdotal story, but it extends to the most acute problems of the Bay Area housing crisis that has become a epitome of inequality. Well intentioned individuals see a compromise and ignore the forest for a couple of trees. There is nothing wrong with caring for those individuals trees, but the government needs to care about the forest and weigh the individual losses accordingly. Individuals from every demographic can do great in the Bay Area and are protected in California, but not consistently or fairly and it comes at the expense of the vast majority who don’t have enough of an individual claim to care about. In California, political vigilantes choose a wedge issue and pursue it with blind vigor and no responsibility for the future outcome of their decisions beyond the immediate effect on their targeted special class. California has a participatory democracy that easily allows individuals to partake in legislative affairs that are normally left to city councils who have to at least have a little care about the long term repercussions of their actions on the area as a whole. This is definitely a hard sell in our current political environment, but legislation should be made by professionals who consider the long term ramifications of the issues at stake not individuals who will always be biased to what is going to effect just their own backyard. What do I think of about the living conditions in San Francisco? I think fixing the living conditions have exceedingly well-understood and viable technical solutions. However, fixing it will appear to cause a little bit of harm to a very sympathy inducing victim, long time home owners, in order to bestow a benefit to everyone including high earning new comers. David needs to lose, but no one has written a sympathetic story for that moral yet.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Golang vs NodeJS vs Python? I am currently working to improve my knowledge and skill to become a back-end developer. Which should I focus more and why?
Answer: All of those languages are actively used so I wouldn’t say any one was a bad choice, but there may be a better choices and better ways to make a choice. First you need to figure out what you want to do on a little more specific level then just back end developer. One way would be to look for places you want to work at with job openings. They will describe the relevant skills they are looking for as well as give you a clue as the types of projects that would be open to you. You could also pick a side project to build on your own and try it in all three languages or look for relevant examples for similar things of what you are wanting to build and pick that one that comes the easiest. In any case, pick a more tangible goal first and your choice should get much clearer.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Will the Republican Tax plan pass as Mc Connell has said?
Answer: A tax plan will almost certainly pass. We still have a year to 2018 elections and republicans will likely control all 3 branches of government after that giving them three years to make good on their promise. I expect progress this year. If not, it will certainly happen before Trump leaves office. Of course we are all looking at the Obamacare repeal efforts and seeing how they crashed and burned. That was different though. Deriding Obamacare was extremely effective at showing the democrats didn’t care about controlling costs, but the reality is there is no easy fix for healthcare and democrats focused on coverage, not cost, with Obamacare. The problem with any healthcare fix is that the losers will be immediately obvious and the winners may not appear for years later. As the democrats knew and found out, any effort to fix healthcare, no matter how effective, is political suicide in the short term. No matter what you do, voters are going to remember the downsides and take the slow and progressive upsides for granted. The Republicans know this and nothing the Republicans floated addressed the major issue with Obamacare, the cost of care. They don’t really want to own healthcare. All the efforts were some form of simple repeal that appealed to their base, but had no practical value to really anyone. It would create enemies of powerful lobbying groups for insurance, hospitals, the AARP, and really do nothing practical for their voters or large political donors. In the short term, costs would go up, while insuring less people. Many Republicans breathed a sigh of relief after legislation moved on from Obamacare fixes which the more politically savvy Republicans saw as a lose-lose situation and something they likely don’t want to revisit until democrats are back in charge and they can stick to simply calling out the bad parts. Any way, tax reform is different. While I think all republicans are on board with lowering tax rates, particularly the corporate tax rates, the way in which it is being done and the amount it is going to add to the deficit has many secretly concerned, just like with repealing Obamacare. However, unlike other Trumpian legislative efforts. Drastically reducing corporate tax rates makes real and practical winners. Winners that are highly correlated with large Republican donors. A lot of the Republican agenda is simply a farce that finds easy victims to blame that don’t actually align with the complexity of reality, nor where the money and political power is. That’s different with tax reform. The winners are palpable and align well with Republican messaging. It may not result in anywhere near the economic growth they claim, but taxes will go down for most people. The costs of which won’t show up for years and after the next election. It will give them a boost for 2018 with their constituents, keep them from getting primaried, and keep their large donor friends. In other words, passing tax reform, no matter how bad for the public at large in the long term, is their only option if they want to keep their job past 2018. 2020 is a different story, but given the number of tea partiers in congress and the guy in the white house now, I think they all realize that there is no rational path to tax reform. It's live with the crazy now, grab what you can while the grabbing is good, and hope for a fix later or just give up. They say the difference between a recession and a depression is that during a recession your neighbor is out of work and in a depression, you are out of work. That’s the choice for for republican’s right now and it's really not much of one if they value being a politician. They may cause a literal recession, but failing to pass any major legislation will put them out of a job. Bend over, tax reform is coming.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why don't we build park-like villages of 500-1000 square foot houses and give them to those who can't afford a housing?
Answer: Better idea. Why don’t we just build housing until it becomes cheap enough that anyone above the poverty line can afford? That means no matter how much you make housing will be cheaper. It’s a win win all around if your goal is to give everyone an affordable place to live. Giving stuff away for free simply creates different winners and losers. Sure it’s great for the person lucky enough to get one, but what about the guy who makes $1 too much. Maybe he makes rent every month, but just barely. Any type of accident or set back is going to devastate him though. He will now have the goal to make slightly less to qualify and those who did qualify certainly are going to want to stay under that limit. Government should come in and build shared infrastructure that’s open to everyone. Building private homes simply distorts a market that would naturally balance itself. This is not a hard problem, we simply need to build housing until it becomes affordable for anyone working the most menial of jobs full time. Doing anything else is stupid prior to fixing that issue.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why does the technology industry receive a disproportionate amount of flack about diversity when other occupations, such as recruitment consultant and warehouse operative, are reportedly more inhospitable to women?
Answer: Why do people focus so much time on acts of terrorism when many more people die in automobile accidents? Why is Beyonce's pregnancy national news when having a child is commonplace? Whether you call it infamy or celebrity, the tech titans have a vaunted place in society. Everyone knows Google and Uber by name. They know what they do and interact with thier products on a daily basis. What's more, the engineering jobs are highly skilled creative pursuits that require motivation, dedication, and responsibility to create a working product and solve unique problems. If your workers are not motivated at a warehouse job, you can just hire some more workers and brute force it. It's a problem, but a more controllable one. If your software engineers make a bad product, it will be seen by customers and have a negative impact on more then just a few worker’s productivity. Culture is very important at tech companies where building a slightly better product can mean whether you survive or not. The perceived value of an engineer also comes from the success of the projects they work on and the visibility of them within the company. Performance is subjective and multiplied by the presence of the deliverables. You can't simply measure performance based on the the number of things you ship or the number of people who get hired from your recruitment activities. As an engineer, if you get put on a project that has a low potential upside, your career will see it's potential drop. Working on a tool to help a handful of administrative employees do thier job just doesn't have the reach of say working on search for Google. If you are made to feel uncomfortable on the project you are on, it may mean switching to a project with a less desirable career trajectory or even have to be down leveled. Switching divisions or jobs means not only a different evironment, but giving up a likely unique project that may hold outsized value to you. Diversity problems in tech companies have an exceptional effect on the company's bottom line, they have an exceptional effect on the employee’s career path, they have some exceptionally undiverse demographics, and the companies in question tend to be exceptionally famous. That doesnt mean diversity issues are unique to tech and if you are an individual experiencing them, it really doesn't matter which industry you are in to make it a problem. Tech is likely far from the most egregious industry. That being said, the tech industry does have a lot of reasons that make it a good place to evolve diversity in the workplace to the next level. Why not start a dialog there?

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: It's often said that if you raise corporate taxes, the business will leave for another state or country. What actually happens to the original state or nation's economy when this happens in the short and long-term?
Answer: In the US the statutory corporate tax rate is relatively disconnected from the effective tax rate corporations pay. Significant changes to the corporate tax rate are almost always accompanied by equally significant changes to deductions and the closing of loopholes. Note both the sharp decline in the statutory rate in the mid 80s is accompanied not by a sharp decline in effective rates, but rather a substantial increase due to closed loopholes! The rest of the timeline is also very disconnected and illustrates that the statutory rate the government sets usually plays only a very tangential role in the effective taxes corporations pay. The health of the overall economy as well as how well corporations are able to restructure to take advantage of the tax code plays a much bigger role as well as the structure of the country’s tax code in question. That doesn’t mean that taxes don’t play a big role in shaping the economy, but the effects tend to be subtle and take decades to play out in ways that can only be completely understood in retrospect and are always way more complicated than as a direct result of a statutory rate change. Incentives and deliberately shaped loopholes tend to be a much bigger driver of where businesses move to. When it comes to taxes, the carrot tends to have way more of a shaping effect on the nation as a whole then the stick. The simple answer to your question as to what happens to the economy as the result of corporate taxes being raised in OECD countries is… nothing happens in the short term. Governments will go out of there way to make sure effective rate increases are minimized when the scrutiny is on after a statutory tax raise and any significant increases are phased in over long periods of time. In the long term, companies will adapt to the new tax code, sometimes in positive ways that match the intention of the behaviors the changes were trying to drive, sometimes in negative ways, the only thing that is clear is that the statutory increase that comes with major changes to the tax code is least predictive metric of the health of the future economy.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: How long would it take an experienced .NET web developer to learn ReactJS and Node.js?
Answer: You should be able to complete a hello world application immediately, but not understand it much. You should be able to slowly fumble your way through architecturally simple real world tasks within a week, be able to write and understand a reasonably complex application in about 3 months and at that point realize almost all of the dumb mistakes you made in the 3 months prior. The next two years will be about getting faster and writing more optimized and reusable code. Also realize that ReactJS and Node.js are fundamentally different things and not any more complimentary then say a ReactJS front end and a .NET restful services backend. You may use Node.js as an integral part of your build chain, but you don’t need much expertise in it to do that. My recommendation would be to use .net for the backend, if possible and react for the front end, then learn Node.js once you have a better understanding of JavaScript as learned through react.

Question: What if I brought a 2017 car to 1960?
Answer: The Jetsons was made in 1962 as a representation of 2062 during the time when most older adults could still remember the era of horse and buggies and yet during that generation they managed to progress to the point of putting a man on the moon. It's still a bit early, but no matter what example of 21st century automobile tech you bring back, it won't fly, it won't fold up into a suitcase, it will have a recognizable power source. Instead of George Jetson's two hour work week, our men work longer hours for less relative pay and we put our women to work for just as long. Our best robots vacuum the floor, but expect you to clean up for them and the ones with a sense of humor are reperitious at best. Our dogs don't talk. The nav system would be nifty, but 50 years to put what seems a step above a TV in the car? You'd get a better reception if you gave a spoiled child coal for Christmas.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: In California, why don’t people sell each other’s homes for a dollar, gift the rest of the value, and then pay low property taxes?
Answer: The price you pay in property taxes is assessed separate from the price the house was sold at. Of course, the home’s selling price typically factors heavily into that assessment and if you paid a bit below the assessed value, you could have a chance of getting it lowered on appeal. If you bought the house for a dollar though, the chances of that are non-existent. The gift tax is also limited to $15k and would also mean you would lose any possibility of a 1031 exchange.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Does the government have the authority to force corporations to use their cash pile to offset the effect of coronavirus? Large cap tech companies are sitting on piles of cash that are really useful in times like this.
Answer: Yes. It’s called the tax code. When the government needs to redistribute wealth or provide a service the private market is unable to implement satisfactorily, the government can change the tax code to incentivize the practice. Want to have a company create medical supplies… create a tax credit for doing so. Want to make sure no one gets laid off, create a tax equal to a years salary that must be paid for anyone laid off in the next year. It can be targeted only at corporations of a certain size or even be a tax on corporate wealth. There are so many possibilities. It’s not a direct seizure of assets, but it doesn’t need to be. Corporations are driven almost solely by profit and taxes hit directly at the bottom line. All it takes is agreement among the three branches of government and the government can get corporations to go in whatever direction they deem fit.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why was global warming (climate change) used as a reason to stop construction of a third runway at Heathrow?
Answer: Airplanes contribute about 2 percent to global warming. If that number seems low, that’s because it is. Most of the world can’t afford to travel by air. For semi-frequent fliers, meaning at least 3 or 4 flights a year, flying contributes more to their carbon footprint then all other sources combined. Flying emits particulate pollution high in the atmosphere that has an additional warming effect. There are lots of factors that effect how polluting plane travel is from the distance of travel, height of travel, efficiency of the plane, to where you sit on the plane, but in virtually all cases it’s the most polluting way to travel sometimes by a 50x margin or more per mile traveled. Worse still, planes are not going to get much greener anytime soon in the future. Where as trains and cars have a clear path to electrification, batteries simply don’t have the energy density appropriate for air travel and using hydrogen or some other source of greener fuel is completely unproven. In other words, the only way we have to make flying greener in any substantial way now, or likely for the next couple of decades, is to simply do less of it. To answer your question, global warming was used as a reason to stop construction at Heathrow, because it happened to be the most legally expeditious way to stop construction. I’m not so naive to believe climate change awareness is more of a motivating factor then pure NIMBYism. With recent regulatory changes though, air travel’s disproportionate contribution to climate change is very easy to prove in court, not because those regulations were written badly, but because it actually is! Much more so then trying to prove irreparable harm from say the noise and disturbance from a few more planes flying over your neighborhood, you can’t move off the earth to escape climate change and there still ain’t no way to unmelt the Antarctic ice sheet that can practically be implemented this millennia. Many other forms of travel exist and this case was not about stopping air travel just limiting it, perhaps just to flights that can’t be easily accomplished by train. Sadly, climate change is not just the best legal reason to stop construction, but is also the most practical reason to stop building it as flying truly is one of the absolute biggest contributors to climate change for the people who use it. The statistics are truly horrendous and make for an easy objective win in court. We just think as coal plants as enemy number one for climate change because so many more people are using coal for their energy needs on a daily basis so the total numbers are simply staggering, but if an individual who flys a few times a year wanted to lessen their carbon footprint, they would be better of putting their efforts into taking other means of transportation then say installing solar panels on their house or shutting down their local coal plant.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: At 61, is it too late to be a founder in a Silicon Valley start-up (received discouraging feedback from 2 known Angels who didn’t hear/read our pitch/deck)? Should we wrap up our 1 year old, self-funded project despite a promising outlook?
Answer: The only way to measure a startup or an idea is with real world metrics measuring user interest. Ideally this is something directly relevant to your idea, like the number of app installs of your product on an MVP, but failing that you can spend a few hundred bucks and run an ad campaign about your idea and set up a marketing site that describes what you are going to do in very glowing terms and see how many e-mails you collect. Feedback from angel investors may contain some very valuable guidance, but it is NOT validation. Digest it. If it makes sense, even if you tend to think otherwise, act on it to try and validate or disprove it. Run some A / B tests with your potential customers and validate who is right… tune your ad campaign or app and see what interest you get back. Opinions about the success of your idea come in all flavors, if you can easily refute discouraging comments, move on. They are worth about 2 grains of salt, about the same as your pitch desk is worth without real world metrics. Smart money, which tend to be VCs, don’t care about ideas or what feedback you got, they care about validation. You want to prove your startup should continue, you need to get out there in front of potential users and get them to take some action that shows they want your product in large numbers. All the feedback in the world from investors won’t validate your product. You should end your startup when you have failed to get positive metrics from real users. You shouldn’t need much money to run a low fidelity campaign, just a bit of creativity and a lot of perseverance.

Question: Which is the world's most dangerous disease? Why?
Answer: My son died of adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD) when he was 8. He was born perfectly normal and had a seemingly perfectly healthy life up until half way through kindergarten. Our first clue came when one of his teachers called us in for a conference to tell us our son, who was for all of his life before that point, exceptionally well behaved, was acting out in school. Nothing particularly mean or even really relatable. He basically just seemed like he was no longer aware of good manners. He would do things like pee outside the urinal or behave erratically at inappropriate times. We had him diagnosed by experts who promptly diagnosed our son with mild autism and ADHD. A bit weird considering he was highly social, reading above level, and prior to this had no real signs of either. We start ABA therapy and do all the things you need to do for a child with special needs. He makes progress he learns to do things better after weeks of intense therapy, but then a few more weeks go by and he gets worse in every way. We didn’t know it then, but he was just relearning to do things with different parts of his brain, not getting better. He starts forgetting things. He’s talking less. He’s climbing furniture and doing immature things he never even did when he was younger. The psychologists imply it’s our fault. We must not be sticking to the therapy. We try harder. Nothing is working. He tells us he has brain freezes and asks us if he’s dying. We tell him of course not, everything is fine, we will work through this and you will get better. Regressions go on for several months. We start to doubt the diagnosis, but there’s nothing we can do except complain to our psychologist who tells us he was misdiagnosed. He actually has severe autism! We ask for a referral to a neurologist to rule out other possibilities. The psychologist refuses, letting us know it’s us. We need to work harder. This goes on for months and we keep on begging for a referral. By the time he is close to non-verbal we finally have another appointment and show the psychologist a video of our son singing and dancing when he was a year younger. It’s a stark contrast to the child we now have who can no longer even attend a regular school. That’s not how autism works. We finally get a referral to a real doctor. We get an MRI and it’s lit up like a Christmas tree. An incredibly intense week of more testing follows. We test for hundreds of different diseases. Finally a genetic test for Adrenoleukodystrophy comes back positive. There’s no doubt. It fits. It’s also a death sentence. There’s no known cure once symptoms start. Over the next year we watch our son forget who we were. Lose the ability to hear, see, smell, taste, and walk. He went through epileptic seizures and eventually became a walking zombie, not really cognizant of the world around him, but still able to perform basic life sustaining tasks like feeding himself. After he ate something he should not have, we had to take him to the ER. The anesthesia, messed with what was left of his brain and he never quite came back. He never walked again after that and could no longer feed himself or really do anything as he lost all of his senses. Once symptoms start, every single person who has ever had this disease dies within a few years at most. Some people have prolonged it by using machines to keep their children alive, but their brains are totally gone except for the autonomic functions. No one has ever reversed the brain damage. The only thing worse then watching your son die is knowing he’s absolutely going to die, knowing he has nothing to live for except more pain and suffering, and the only way to stop the suffering is to starve him to death. We had a team of doctors at that point. Not helping our son. There was nothing they could do for him and his body was actually quite healthy. He was just in a semi vegetative state. Awake, but not cognizant of the world around him. His soul was actually the first thing to go. His behaviors changed and for all intents and purposes, the disease took our son’s identity and dignity before any of the more physical ailments. There was no hope he was still in there. No question he was gone for over a year. This team of doctors was there for us, his parents, to guide us through his death. They were his palliative care team. We were at Stanford and they were some of the most qualified, compassionate, and intelligent doctors I have encountered. Near the end, I wanted to punch every one of them. It wasn’t their fault. They are messengers in a broken system, but they all knew our son was dying. They all knew his brain function was gone. They all knew he was never coming back. The adrenoleukodystrophy expert actually told us down to the month when our son would lose each of his functions. He was incredibly accurate. The last few meetings we had were all about how removing nutrition and hydration isn’t so bad, hes past where he is aware of most things. The body “knows” it’s dying and just peacefully gives up. It all felt made up. They said they will control the pain with morphine. Fuck! I know what morphine does. My first question is what is the point of prolonging his life. Theres no answers of hope coming back, no answers of he might still be there. Just the elephant in the room no one explicitly brings up. Society says this is the only path. “It’s fine.” But it wasn’t fine. My next question was how much morphine will stop all the pain immediately forever. They wouldn’t answer that one. My son died when he was 8 after 3 weeks without food or water. Adrenoleukodystrophy is a rare genetic disease. It can be cured if it's caught with a test before symptoms start with a simple genetic test at birth. The federal government recommended this test before my son was born to be included with all newborn screenings. No state at the time he was born adopted the test as part of newborn screening despite that it pays for itself. When he died only 5 states did, today 44 do. If you have a son that was born with the gene for ALD, 1/3rd develop adrenoleukodystrophy most of the rest develop a related disorder that has very serious symptoms that start in the 20s or 30s. 10% have just minor adrenal gland issues that are treatable. This is a photo of the last time I was able to get Griffin to laugh. He was otherwise non-verbal at this point, and struggling with a lot of his senses, but often you would barely know it if you saw us out. Physically his body was healthy. He was mobile nearly to the end. The one saving grace about the progression of his disease is that he seemed to lose the ability to comprehend death and other abstract concepts early. We wasted so much precious time with the misdiagnosis. Nothing will ever make up for that, but I’m glad we tried. Happy Father's Day!

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Unfortunately, Elon Musk cancelled all remote work because work from home does not work. Does that mean as a propeller of artificial intelligence, he is unrealistic?
Answer: I am a software architect. I have worked at startups both inside and outside of Silicon Valley . I have been one of the highest level of employees at a Fortune 500 tech company that still had a direct part in making the sausage. I have spent over a decade being in an office and almost as much time working remotely. I have founded a startup that grew from nothing to millions in revenue in a couple of years. I have been the lead software developer on projects that have grown from nothing to 100 million dollar businesses. More importantly, I have failed spectacularly in a multitude of ways and experienced first hand what doesn’t work. I have also rescued multiple projects that were driven into the ground that would have been cancelled otherwise and turned them into revenue producing beasts. I am now a consultant and my work comes mostly from that reputation. I work remotely and the project I have been on most recently for a number of years now may be the most productive for revenue per engineering hour spent. Suffice it to say, I can tell you working remotely, not only works, it works better for certain roles on certain projects. Like everything else, the details matter and there are some projects better suited to remote work then others. Musk’s remote work policy is a bit naive as a general rule of thumb and sounds basically like a plan for grossly control chaos. It is a recipe for success at startups where most of your employees have to wear multiple hats and do whatever needs to get done to make something work and more importantly, it matters much less if you piss off your existing customer base by releasing a feature that will revolutionize it. Working remotely is the best for detailed oriented work where the business model is well known and precise engineering is required. It’s less valuable when your business plan hinges on blindly throwing darts at a board and finding the one that sticks. The latter usually means you are doing some crazy implementation and ignoring some general rules to get something novel out quickly. Being in person becomes more helpful to maintain speed and let your teammates know not just the technical direction you are going, but to better appreciate how your mind works so they can quickly compliment it at that point in time even though no one truly understands the full implications yet. That type of work less successful at large enterprises where revenue growth tends to be driven more by wowing existing customers by mostly keeping the wheels on and spinning at 100mph. Those customers love new features that compliment their existing workflows, but absolutely hate it when features change that they have built their business around. Musk saw that hate firsthand when he came into Twitter and shook things up. That being said, it might not actually be a bad move. It’s definitely risky and kudos to Musk for putting his own money and resources on the line to fix a really tricky problem. Twitter seemingly more or less saturated it’s market and was stuck at where it was and hemorrhaging cash. Not to mention Twitter was becoming a target and more and more hated by the general public on both sides of the political aisle just for doing its job. An explosive shake up and a return to a startup mentality may be the only thing that can get the company back to growth so its hard to really call Musk out at Twitter for his tactics. They have been immediately negative, no doubt, but I can see long term success if he plays his cards right. Tesla, on the other hand, is now a finely tuned enterprise that has vey successful products and a robust roadmap that should keep them growing hugely well into the future. They seem to be struggling with execution just as completion from the big auto companies is heating up in their segment. They need to focus on simply delivering value to their existing customers. They need incremental change now. Tesla’s engineering employees would do well to relax, work smarter, not harder and focus on the detailed oriented work of simply making existing processes work better. They should be focused on the hard facts. They should largely know the path they just have to execute it well without a lot of noise. That’s they core value for remote work. It is the home of the mundane where you can be comfortable working long hours on relatively boring stuff that has to get done. A remote worker doesn’t have a physical presence in front of their boss and coworkers to prove they are working, they just have their output. It has to work and be done well otherwise your excuses sound only like excuses. In any case, this is the real world, there is both a place for remote work and in office work. Musk is both a brilliant CEO and flawed human. He’s taking huge risks that may or may not pay off and he makes mistakes. I actually think he would be best served by empowering a new CEO at Tesla to take the reigns and do the boring things to grow the company that Musk is very Ill suited for. He should drop his public highly partisan political statements, but otherwise shake the bird till it either dies or flies at Twitter. As to your actual question, let me just state the obvious… the reality of artificial intelligence is that no one knows what it takes to get to a general all around human-like level of intelligence. We have spent enough time growing the technology to know that just knowing what good enough looks like in an AI is in itself a very hard problem. We will know it when we see it and live with it and it’s flaws for a while. That type of thing is totally unpredictable and yes Musk or anyone else saying they know a timeline for AI performing at acceptable levels for currently impossible task for computers is unknowable. It also has nothing to do with Musk’s stance on remote work.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: When taking a computer science course, how can you determine what content is extremely important to my future as a software developer, and what exercises are just training me on how to solve problems at hand?
Answer: Don’t sweat the details. Learn the stuff to get the grade, then make sure you code on the side as much as possible. No new grad should show up to an interview without significant coding experience on real world projects. When I interview someone, I don’t care about what theory you know, I care about if you know how to use it in the real world effectively and that goes for new grads. Coding is a virtually free way to produce a new product. You have no excuse for not having a few projects to your name even if no one has ever paid you to build anything. The important stuff you learn you’ll repeat often and retain it pretty quickly. You are also never going to be able to stop learning either. Custom software development is about doing things no one has done before and that’s often only possible using new libraries that push the state of the art and have to be learned a new. The theory you learn in school will help you connect those dots, but you will only have to retain a cursory understanding of them to apply it to the new stuff you will have to learn. My advice to you is if you have free time and studied enough to pass your tests, don’t waste anymore time on trying to understand the theory, just code. Put your skills to use and make something. There are no words or tutorials that can show you what’s important better then actually trying to produce something real and seeing where the pain points are.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Which things about Silicon Valley were most unbelievable when you talked to people back home?
Answer: That you can be making $500k a year and still questioning if you can afford a starter home.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What’s the net pay for a renter making $185K in California filing single with no dependents?
Answer: You’ll pay about $70k in taxes. Leaving you with $115k. Max out your retirement and you’ll have $97k. After renting a not great, but decent place for $2500 a month, you’ll have $67k. A decent newish car will cost you $8k a year with fuel, insurance, etc. Assume another $2k a month for food and necessities like Netflix and internet access. That leaves you with $37k. Dump that into savings and in 8 years you may have enough for a down payment for a house in one of California’s urban areas.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Would you take a career in the Bay Area if you don't have outside financial support or are not in tech?
Answer: Whether you are in tech or not matters less and less every year. Your average software developer here makes around $125k even in the higher paying areas. It's quite possible to do substantially better in tech, but that is a game that involves both lots of skill and lots of luck and isn’t implicit with simply having a tech job. $125k doesn’t make buying any home in the area within an hour commute remotely affordable. Marry someone who makes that and you will be able to scrape the bottom of the barrel though, but as real estate increases in cost far in excess of the raises those in tech are receiving, that gets harder and harder and it puts most tech people in the same boat as everyone else in the Bay Area, wondering how they will ever be able to afford to live here or move up to a place that matches their new family needs. People in tech may be better off on average, but for most it’s like being the best player on the last place team. You want to be on the winning team, not just be good and still losing. That’s not to say there isn’t ample opportunity in the Bay Area some of which are unique to the area, but that doesn’t apply to just tech. The money here drives a lot of careers downstream. Again, though, it comes down to being at the top of your game and lucky if you want to achieve a middle class family life style. There is no sure win no matter the field. You can make it big here, you can also play the game and sacrifice a lot of your quality of living to save big on a high salary thats modest for the area, but otherwise pretty significant and allows you to move up if you can some day move out. My point though, is its shitty for everyone new to the area when using traditional financing and typical family life goals. Being in tech alone doesn’t get you past that. Creative living arrangements, moxy, and a drive to be the best can no matter the field and the desire to take on those burdens is way more important than what you do.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Forget warp speed, why is it so hard to get to even 1% of the speed of light with modern (or even near future tech) whether manned or unmanned? Is it that hard to come up with a new fuel source better than rocket fuel?
Answer: Ultimately, there is no practical reason to go faster given its cost. 1% the speed of light is about 7 million miles an hour. That’s unfathomably fast. 100x faster then the fastest rocket that takes enormous boosters to get to that speed. We’ve gotten pretty close going 400,000 miles an hour with a gravitational assist from the sun. That takes time though, but 1% the speed of light seems achievable. There are various ideas that could get us that fast, but when you need billions of dollars to go relatively slow, the real thing that makes going faster hard is why? With time we can get to every planet in our solar system and have done just that well within a human lifetime. Getting there faster would certainly help, but getting a budget is more of a problem then waiting decades for the result. The best use of limited money is to do more science slower rather then less faster. Speed wouldn’t really help our currently feasible missions given the cost. Now of course the reason to go really really fast is to get to places we haven’t been to. The problem is even going to speed of light isn’t terribly helpful. Space to just too damn big. We are 12 years away from the closest interesting extra solar planet at the speed of light. That’s 1200 years away at 1% the speed of light. Its also likely not any more interesting then Venus, which we have barely explored. That’s the closest, the top 100 list of interesting planets ends at thousands of light years away. Quite simply even if we could go the speed of light, it would still take an extraordinary amount of luck to find some place more interesting then the planets we have in our own solar system. In other words, until we discover new laws of physics that would let us change the maximum speed at which matter can travel, well beyond the speed of light, going faster doesn’t matter, practically speaking, the speed of light is just too damn slow to be worth a damn in the vastness of space.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why can't we end public transportation? Why should the taxes of the rest of the normal country go to subsidize the cost of living of a urban minority who are already higher paid on average? Just compare wages in upstate and downstate.
Answer: Building infrastructure to transport just a ~200lb person is substantially cheaper then building infrastructure to support a 2 ton car as long as you have the ridership to support public transportation. Public transportation is actually a great deal for tax payers on a per capita basis assuming each person that takes the train would otherwise be driving a car. The real estate public street parking occupies alone would pay for all the public transportation needs several times over. If you want to reduce taxes we should spend more on public transportation, not less. We spend stupidly large amounts of money supporting cars in cities. Often in places when they average movement of less then 10 mph. However if you want to talk about subsidies, you will find much greater spending on a per capita basis going to rural areas that build miles and miles of roads for just a handful of individuals. Cities are actually way more efficient for people to live. Not to mention those city dwellers pay substantially more in taxes as their incomes tend to be higher.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: As a programmer/software developer, do you prefer sitting or standing desks at work?
Answer: Standing all day is hard. Sitting all day is less hard. I choose sitting despite having generous access to standing desks. While some may argue standing is better exercise, being the smug asshole programmer trying to fit into my stereotype that I am, I am happy to point out, standing is not exercise as you are not moving. The other health benefits are a mixed bag. The important thing is to change up any repetitive activity periodically. If a standing desk helps you with that, go for it and don’t let anyone call you a hipster. As to me, I like to change up my sitting by laying down and taking a nap. I call that my exercise.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Is Lexus the lowest quality of luxury cars?
Answer: Thats a silly question. You might as well ask what color of car is the best. The biggest driver of quality tends to be cost. Quality varies somewhat between brands, but you can’t possibly wrap the quality of a brand that encompasses everything from low 5 figures to ones that are well into the 6 figures into a practical opinion on the brand in general. Brands are 99% marketing. The big ones are highly commoditized and they take very few chances particularly on their bread and butter vehicles. If you want to judge quality, look at the specific models and even more so go test drive a car with a particular option package yourself. Form your own opinions on the style and get specific reviews on particular models from well respected sources like consumer reports. Ignore the brand when it comes to quality though. All the major brands have had a model or two that were real lemons. The badge on the front of the car, isn’t going to be able shine up one of those turds.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: If you live in California and are working on a side project, and then take a new full time position, how do you prevent the new company from owning your side project?
Answer: Every large company I have worked for usually asks you to declare any inventions or preexisting IP you have in your employment contract when you start with them. Fill that out and don’t make a big deal about it. You start asking specific hypothetical questions and they will refer you to the legal department which will find risk with hiring you if you give them a reason. Otherwise as long as your project is broadly unrelated to your day job, you shouldn’t have a problem and I’ve never had anyone in management who wasn’t supportive as long as I made it clear I was only working on it in my free time. You can also let your manager know at any time you started working on a side project in your free time at any point after you start working and he will likely have you fill out a declaration. Even if you don’t do that, there likely be won’t be any questions asked when you quit especially if it’s on good terms. Just don’t burn any bridges or do something blatently unethical. The few times that I heard of IP conflicts with employees that led to lawsuits was when either the employee was blatantly stealing IP and bragging about it or there was another somewhat unrelated suit between companies and the lawyers tossed in a stolen IP accusation from an employee who happened to be at both companies.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Is an associates in graphic design valuable when trying to become a front end web developer?
Answer: I've looked over hundreds of resumes and made hiring decisions on lots of developers. What I look for is past experience. Assuming you have that and it's relevant, you have likely already earned yourself an interview already in 90% of the cases. Relevance is not a discreet thing though and usually you find people that come close. If you are in that iffy case, you'll get tossed in the proceed pile if your education or academic background is strong. A graphic design degree would likely not qualify unless you got it from an Ivy league or someplace that really stood out. Then I might give you a chance or if for some reason your relevance was low, but still better then any other candidates you'd also get through. The degree may actually make your interview harder though as I would press you more on coding questions that designers are not likely to encounter when doing some light coding to make sure you have fully committed to being an engineer. In any case, your associates isn't worthless. It's better then no degree or something like a philosophy degree, but I'm going to be impressed more by a project, no matter how simple, implemented using the technology we are looking to hire for. That being said I'm not HR and havimg a degree can be more of a gate and the associates may be the difference of whether it makes it to me or not, but in general with development, you are going to be judged way more on your experience and specific akills then your academic record. Frontend development also crosses over into design quite often and having design skills and demonstrating they are compatible with whatever design process we have would be a real win. The associates will speak to that, but not much more then a portfolio would. Some positions at smaller companies explicitly look for candidates who can both design and code and your degree would be a real boon in those rare cases, but again in the majority of cases, your tech skills are going to be sole thing that gets you hired as a developer.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Is it a good idea to buy homes in cities where monthly rents match up (or are more) to mortgage payments?
Answer: It's risky. Whether it's good or bad will be a function of how long you stay in the house and how much it appreciates. Rents typically tail home prices so a city with a mortgage payment less then rent is likely one on the decline. In the short term, you may see a double digit percent of loss in your homes value immediately after buying that locks you in and could be precipitously bad if the decline comes from a recession in which you experience a job loss. On the converse you may double your investment in a short period. It's impossible to tell what will happen especially looking at just rent vs housing prices for metrics. If this is your primary household, don't look at it as an investment. It's a good idea to buy a house regardless of the rent vs buy metrics, if you can afford it and can see yourself living in it for a decade or more. Full stop. Don't over think it, assuming your following the standard advice of a 20% down mortgage and the house appraised, that's all you need to consider. Anything else may not prove to be a bad idea, but you aren't going to know that just by looking at the relative mortgage to rent costs. In other words, whether it's a good idea or not should be a function of how much you will like the house long term, not whether the investment will deliver.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Is Google building housing for its employees in Silicon Valley in 2018? How much will they charge?
Answer: They are building housing. It won't be enough to change the price of housing even if they are allowed to build 10,000+ units. The housing will be priced at market rates which will likely be $3k for a 1 bd, $4k for a 2 bd, $5k for a 3 bd. I could also see them going for slightly above market rates as the lack of commute and amenities will probably be worth a premium. My guess is it will be almost impossible to get them, like any place around here, they will be on the market for less then 30 days and if you want one, you will have to sign a lease immediately when it becomes available.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What do you think of "San Francisco Bay Area cities are cracking down on free food at tech companies — here’s why that’s a good idea, according to a startup cofounder"?
Answer: Restaurants in the Bay Area are suffering because they can’t find enough employees who can afford to live there and work on a waitresses salary. Giving them more customers seems a poor fix , particularly ones use to getting food for free and will balk at going out if lunch starts to cost $20. Build more housing, then maybe we can talk about the restaurants. If you really want to create a vibrant downtown with lots of restuarants, build some tall residential buildings, make the first floor retail and restuarants. You don’t have to force corporations to operate against thier interests and you solve the real problem to boot.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: How should I start a freelance career as a web designer & programmer? How do I not be cheated?
Answer: You need to build a network of customers. That’s hard to do by cold calling, particularly if your skills are in building amazing web applications that speak for themselves and less so in selling abstract ideas like your personal brand. The most common way to build a network is to work as a full time employee for several years and develop a reputation as an independent problem solver who can figure what needs to be done, then do it. You can have a specialty, but it should be a general specialty, like UI programmer or designer. Being the best jQuery or other framework developer ever is worse than just being known as a solid developer who always delivers. Build strong relationships with the people who make hiring decisions or those exemplary employees who seem like they are going places. Diversify and bounce around every couple of years either in company or outside of it. Make as many professional friends as possible. You will know you have succeeded when at any point in time, you can think of three past associates who you could call who would likely have a opportunity they could offer to you and would love to work with you again. You will almost never have to worry about being cheated if you do work for your friends who work as large, stable companies as long as you do good work. Getting paid on time, is a whole other can of worms, but large companies almost always pay up as long as you do your part and provide well documented invoices.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why do computer manufacturers purposely complicate the process of adding new components? Why not just add convenient "RAM" slots on the exterior?
Answer: Ram use to be expensive and a real bottleneck. If you didn't have enough ram you couldn't run a particular program and many times you didn't realize that until after you bought the computer and had it for several months when a new application comes out. That is no longer the case. Today, you get at least 4 Gbs in even bottom of the line machines and that amount does what most people want just fine. Even 8 Gb of value ram will cost manufacturers less than $20. In fact, adding more ram by default can be cheaper then adding the ability to add more ram in the future. We know how much ram the vast majority of even power users use on modern operating systems and it tends to max out at 8 Gb. More solves problems for exceedingly few users doing a few very specific tasks. Manufacturers don’t add convenient RAM slots today because people would expect their computers to get faster or more capable when they used them. Today if you add more ram to a slow PC, you will still just end up with a slow PC with more ram.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why doesn't WebAssembly support DOM access? What design challenges would the people making it possible to access the DOM face?
Answer: I think the first problem is that I don’t really think it’s a design challenge, it sounds more like a requirements problem that comes from a fundamental misunderstanding of the value that WebAssembly brings. The only reason to put yourself through the interop hell that is webassembly is for performance and DOM access is one of the slowest things you do in web development. It is the bottleneck that makes almost all other tasks you do in native JavaScript seen orders of magnitude faster. If you are manipulating the DOM you might as well just use JavaScript. It might add a few milliseconds to your runtime, but that is unnoticable to the hundreds of milliseconds your DOM access will require. You don’t want to make DOM access easy from WebAssembly as people may just start to use it for direct DOM manipulation instead of simply doing the simple thing and using JavaScript for that. If any computation heavy work needs to be done, you can send that off to WebAssembly, then do your DOM manipulation in JavaScript once you get your answer back and your sandbox is less restrictive and way more feature rich. Despite that, I am sure some genius will build some tools that do make it much easier to manipulate the DOM from WebAssembly. That doesn’t mean it’s a good idea though even if there are a handful of legitimate uses.

Question: When will liberals care about Hunter Biden considering all his crimes?

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why is socialism so popular with young Americans even though it worked nowhere?
Answer: You are watching too much fox news. Get out in the real world and actually talk to someone young. I have never heard any statement uttered to the effect that we should get rid of all privately owned companies and let the government handle all means of production. By anyone in the real world. Not even anything remotely suggesting that. There is perhaps no more universal belief in this country among both young and old that it should be based on capitalism. You need to realize it is perfectly acceptable to believe the government can do better and more then it is doing now and still believe in capitalism. Regulation and capitalism are not mutually exclusive. They go hand in hand. Regulation ensures a smooth running economy over the long term. If that’s not a goal of capitalism, I don’t know what is. The young people I met simply think the government can control excessive pursuits of profit at the expense of society better then the market will self regulate. That’s a really painfully obvious common sense statement. If you want to have a legimate discussion, it needs to be on where the line should be on that regulation. You are the only one talking about socialism and, as a young person, it’s hard to relate to you when you start talking about such crazy things.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: To retain grandfathered Prop. 13 property tax benefit, can you trade houses with your friend in a different state (both of you occupying the other's house) without changing prospective ownerships of said houses?
Answer: California is the only state stupid enough to have a property tax tied to the purchase price of a house and not the true market price so only one of you will get the benefit. It's not tied to income or residency. It's a giveaway to property owners no matter how rich, which nation you are a citizen of, whether you are a multi billion dollar corporation, or where you actually live. No worries, as long as you don't sell the property, you will get to take advantage.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Why is San Jose such a shithole with such an extraordinary tax base and Silicon Valley right next door?
Answer: The tax base is only extraordinary in how unequal it is. San Jose is in California and it has prop 13 and oddly regressive income taxes. New residents get absolutely hammered with taxes as existing ones only pay property taxes on the amount they paid for a place which is often several times less then what it’s worth now. Income taxes are both state and local and rise with rising income. Those existing residents may also be making far less then what it would take to move into the area. All this equates to a highly variable tax base. Many areas are shitty because a great number of residents pay next to nothing in property taxes regardless of how much they make or what they do. It also applies to corporations and all those startups tend to lease thier space from a corporation that’s paying taxes on thier assess value in 1970. Corporations use to pay 50% of property tax revenues, it’s now closer to 25%. Quite simply areas are shitty because they have no money. Those new tech people may be paying through the roof to live thier, but 20% of the population can’t make up for the remaining 80% paying next to nothing. The area also struggles with a highly progressive agenda that sometimes prioritizes homeless shelters and generous government pension plans over things like fixing aging infrastructure.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Is there anyone who still enjoys living in the Bay Area? All the forums have a lot of negatives and talk about people moving away in droves.
Answer: Of course. The negatives of the Bay Area are driven by profound inequality. The haves here have it really good at the expense of everyone else. If you are lucky enough to call yourself a homeowner, congratulations, the average equity in your home went up by more then the average worker grossed in income from working. On top of that, your property taxes raise at less then the rate of inflation so you get a built in raise every year too just for staying by at home, doing nothing. Yeah, the traffic sucks for everyone, but less so for those who live in a single family home that’s walking distance from amenities you would only find in dense urban areas elsewhere. What’s more, California’s constitution gives ordinary citizens substantial veto power to determine what gets built in their town. If you are a renter, all those things make it so you can barely make ends meet on large six figure salary. That sucks and sucks more knowing that the substantial taxes you pay don’t go to making CA this liberal Mecca where everyone gets treated equally, but instead goes to a fortunate few of the previous generation to subsidize thier own homes that are larger then what you could ever dream of affording here. Lots of people do better in the Bay Area then they would anywhere else in the nation. It has great weather, great jobs, lots of things to do, and suburban living that is comfortable, but defies all societal sensibilities. The Bay Area has few downsides when you don’t have to worry about the cost of living. Unfortunately, if you want to fix the bad things you are going to have to tear down some of the things causing the inequality that some people love.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: What is an average rent increase in Sunnyvale, CA? Should you expect to pay more every year?
Answer: No. Rent in Sunnyvale is relatively stable compared to home prices which have been going up 10% to 20% every year. Homebuyers in the area tend to see much more value in a home purchase then a renters see in living here as a substantial part of the value of a home here is based on speculative growth potential not simply as a nice place to live. Most workers who live in Sunnyvale can’t remotely afford to purchase a place at current market rates and rental rates are more tied to average incomes. That doesn’t mean it’s cheap to rent. Rent is now affordable only to high earning tech workers or those on comparable salaries, but it’s still an incredible deal compared to a mortgage on a typical single family home. A mortgage here can be 2 or 3 times the average rent and is getting worse. Unlike a typical market, rent is not tightly coupled to the rise in home values, but rather salaries, which don’t go up at the same rate. If things continue going well for the economy at about the same pace they have been, expect a rent increase every other year, maybe every 3 or more years renting from an individual. It will likely be around 5% and closely tied the inflation.
